entries.title: AnyVIO: Feed-Forward Streaming Visual-Inertial Odometry Across Platforms
entries.abstract: Geometric foundation models (GFMs) estimate camera mo- tion and scene structure from images without requiring ex- pert parameter tuning, but either lack metric scale or rely on learned priors to infer scale, which is unobservable from monocular images alone. Inertial sensing offers a way to observe metric scale, but existing methods add inertial in- formation through a filter or factor graph, which reintro- duces bespoke parameter tuning and optimization costs that can grow with the trajectory. To bridge this gap, we present AnyVIO, a real-time, feed-forward streaming model for monocular visual-inertial odometry (VIO), which combines a streaming GFM with an inertial foundation model (IFM). Both the GFM and IFM predict the metric motion between consecutive frames, and a lightweight learned fusion head quantifies the reliability of each estimate and blends them in a single forward pass. Across nine datasets recorded from cars, legged and ground robots, and handheld and head- mounted devices, AnyVIO reduces the metric position error of its visual model by 36% while publishing each pose esti- mate 70 ms after an image is received. We further deploy AnyVIO onboard two real vehicles at up to 140 km/h, where it remains accurate in poor lighting and heavy dust.

entries.title: Susceptibility source separation via Closed-form Alternating Newton-type Optimization
entries.abstract: Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping (QSM) provides a bulk magnetic susceptibility estimate per voxel, so contributions from paramagnetic and diamagnetic sources within the same voxel partially cancel. Susceptibility source separation methods identify these compartments by fitting a three-pool complex exponential model to multi-echo gradient-echo (GRE) data. However, conventional voxel-wise fitting with general-purpose constrained solvers requires several hours per whole-brain volume and often fails in high-susceptibility regions. We present CANON-QSM (Closed-form Alternating Newton-type Optimization for QSM), a solver that reformulates the subproblems of the three-pool model and solves them alternately via exact closed-form updates and Newton-type steps, yielding a substantial per-voxel computational speedup. Both in silico and in vivo evaluations demonstrate not only a massive reduction in reconstruction time, completing a whole-brain volume in under two minutes, but also improved accuracy and robustness against artifacts in high-susceptibility regions. Finally, an echo-time analysis of the three-pool model shows that source separation is driven by second-order nonlinearities in signal decay and phase evolution rather than first-order bulk estimates.

entries.title: From power to spectrum: an off-the-shelf photodiode turned into a spectrometer by its bias alone
entries.abstract: Computational spectrometers replace dispersive optics with detectors whose spectral response can be varied, but every reported single-detector device obtains this response through dedicated fabrication: two-dimensional heterostructures, graded epitaxial junctions, organic stacks, filters or photonic circuits. We demonstrate a generic, fabrication-free alternative in which a standard commercial photodiode becomes a spectrometer through its electrical drive alone, requiring no modification of the device, no optical filter and no modulation of the light. The mechanism is bias-modulated optoelectronic chromatic dispersion (OED): light of different wavelengths is absorbed at different depths, and a sinusoidal bias changes how carriers generated at each depth are collected, so that every spectrum is encoded in the shape of the photocurrent waveform over one bias period. Applied to an unmodified InGaAs PIN photodiode at room temperature, a 10 us waveform decoded by a neural network reconstructs spectra of one to three laser lines across the 80 nm of the telecom C+L band, locating the lines to 0.3-0.4 nm, counting them in about 99% of measurements and identifying their power levels, with line shifts tracked to tens of picometres. Because OED relies on universal semiconductor transport physics, the approach is material-agnostic and applies in principle to any off-the-shelf photodiode, turning detectors already deployed as power monitors into low-cost spectral sensors.

entries.title: Deterministic Temporal Embedding for Calcium Imaging Trace Extraction
entries.abstract: Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embedding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to a low-dimensional representation in which temporally coherent sources form spatially coherent regions. Starting from a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, we optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decomposition of the dense repulsive interaction with sparse edge compensation, avoiding stochastic negative sampling. The resulting latent representation is spatially decoded into reliable source supports for trace extraction without imposing an explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources together with efficient deterministic embedding optimization.

entries.title: OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture Beyond the Camera Frame Rate
entries.abstract: For 4D reconstruction, a synchronized multi-camera rig records all views at the same timestamps and misses the motion between them. Staggered triggers spread the same frames over more timestamps. However, when the cameras along each row fire one after another, as in 4DSloMo's schedule on the N3DV rig, the row acts as one moving camera that confounds depth with motion. We introduce OffBeat, which models a staggered rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler: shifted copies of one sampling grid. From the calibration alone, OffBeat derives camera groups that fire together and their firing order. Since one group records each timestamp, a short-lived primitive can fit an error its cameras share, such as a color offset, and flicker in novel views. We show that a primitive's opacity over time weights all groups equally, for every number of groups, only if it lasts at least one camera frame interval. On Spacetime Gaussians, a minimum lifetime approximates this bound, and a closed-form smoothed box of that length satisfies it exactly, with less flicker than a Gaussian in its place at nearly equal PSNR. In simulated staggered capture on N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline with video diffusion on every test frame, by 3.04 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR. Between the first and last synchronized frame, it outperforms the best synchronized method of each scene, with or without frame interpolation, by 1.98 dB in mean dynamic-region PSNR, while synchronized capture is better at its own frames. On PanopticSports, in this frame range, OffBeat is comparable in PSNR to synchronized capture with interpolation. On every N3DV scene, replacing 4DSloMo's schedule with ours raises the dynamic-region PSNR of Spacetime Gaussians, 4DSloMo without diffusion, and our reconstruction. Multi-camera rigs could follow faster motion at the same frame count by changing only when each camera fires.

entries.title: FirstCross: Convex Single-Photon 3D Reconstruction from Sparse Views
entries.abstract: Single-photon lidar records the arrival time of each returning photon, enabling 3D reconstruction from few views and scarce photons. However, leading neural methods such as Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization, and their accuracy degrades as photon flux decreases. We propose FirstCross, a network-free approach that instead solves a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid. For a solid object, the Poisson likelihood of a ray with given signal and background rates depends on the scene solely through its first crossing, the point where the ray first enters the object. Decomposing this likelihood yields two tractable terms. The first penalizes surfaces in front of detected photons and admits a tight convex closure, namely volume rendering with a running-maximum transmittance in place of NeRF's product transmittance. The second accounts for photons that no surface explains and admits a convex upper bound once the object is assumed to be thick behind each detected surface point. Compared with Transientangelo under its own real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across every test scene, view count, and flux level. With three views and 100 times fewer photons than at the protocol's lowest flux, our mean object depth error stays under half of Transientangelo's with all photons. Given our detected surface points, the best classical fusion has 1.3 to 1.8 times our three-view error across flux levels. On real room-scale captures with 1% of their photons, TransientNeRF has 2.8 to 7.7 times our error. FirstCross lets few-view single-photon scanners cut exposure to 1% and reconstruct an object in about a minute on one GPU.

entries.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
entries.abstract: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.
entries.comment: 13 pages (incl. cover page), 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted version of the article published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. Please cite the published version (DOI: 10.1109/TBME.2026.3666306). Code: https://github.com/Stef-Martin/E2E-MRE
entries.journalRef: IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering (2026), early access

entries.title: MambaLIFT: Reference-Based Mechanism-Aware Attribution for VMamba
entries.abstract: Attributing predictions of visual state-space models remains challenging because input-dependent selective dynamics couple feature selection, recurrent state propagation, and shared computational pathways. We introduce MambaLIFT, a reference-based, multiplier-first attribution framework for VMamba that propagates contributions through its computational graph using interaction-aware rules for selective-scan injection, recurrent memory, LayerNorm, and shared pathways. MambaLIFT decomposes the reference-relative class-logit difference, f_c(x)-f_c(x⁰), by spatial position, VSS block, scan direction, and computational mechanism. Experiments on ImageNet-1K evaluate VMamba-T and VMamba-B, with hyperparameters selected on a calibration set and faithfulness assessed on a disjoint held-out evaluation set. MambaLIFT achieves numerical conservation to floating-point precision across audited attribution interfaces in both configurations. Under mean-colour pixel flipping, it achieves significantly higher mean faithfulness scores than MambaLRP on both configurations and the highest scores among the evaluated methods, including Integrated Gradients with matched references. Under blurred replacement, MambaLIFT is non-inferior to MambaLRP on VMamba-T and equivalent on VMamba-B, indicating that its advantage depends on the replacement protocol. Ablations on VMamba-T show that interaction allocation, temporal propagation, and pathway composition affect attribution maps. Mechanism-level analyses further show that exact relevance conservation does not imply additive effects under finite interventions: the mechanism decomposition accounts for the reference-relative logit difference but does not estimate intervention effects or establish causal validity.

entries.title: Passing NPCR Without Diffusion: Exact Signatures, a Detection Benchmark and an Audit of Published Image Ciphers
entries.abstract: NPCR, the share of ciphertext bytes changed by a one-pixel plaintext change, is reported for nearly every image cipher as evidence of diffusion, with 99.61% the target. Several mechanisms produce values near it, and the mean does not say which. We separate three regimes: no propagation, one round of forward and backward chaining linear over addition or XOR, and independent ciphertexts. For the second an exact count applies. After a least-significant-bit change its mean asymptotically matches the independent-ciphertext reference, while its spread without cancellation is about five to twenty times larger. In simulation, the one-sided NPCR test of Wu, Noonan and Agaian flags one-round additive, mixed and S-box chaining in 2-4% of papers; read in both directions, the same five values flag at least 99.9%. Two-sided testing does the detecting; the spread and the other signatures help diagnose the structure. We then audit twenty-one published schemes. The count matches a reimplementation of one published diffusion layer on every trial and accounts for its reported table, the signatures show two schemes whose printed specifications cannot produce their reported values, and find that three of our own report plain-versus-cipher values and fall to two chosen images; ten more change their encryption material with the plaintext or per encryption, so their NPCR mostly reflects that change. A released checker applies the signatures to published tables, showing what a table measures within stated assumptions; it does not certify security.
entries.comment: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Information Security and Applications. This is the submitted version; the accepted manuscript will replace it once the article's DOI is available. 31 pages, 5 figures, 16 tables. Code and records: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22796547

entries.title: LBW-NPS: A Local Band-Weighted Noise Power Spectrum Loss for Texture-Preserving Low-Dose CT Denoising
entries.abstract: Low-dose CT denoising should suppress noise while retaining the local texture of the reference image. Matching a pooled spectrum can overlook regional discrepancies, whereas pixel losses alone can favor overly smooth outputs. We propose a local band-weighted noise power spectrum loss (LBW-NPS) that compares spectral energies within overlapping Hann-tapered patches, without tissue-specific loss conditioning. Each valid patch contributes a weighted squared log-energy difference across three frequency bands, alongside an L₁ reconstruction term. We compare LBW-NPS against L₁-only training and five auxiliary-loss baselines using the same U-Net and three seeds on DeepLesion slices with simulated low-dose acquisitions, including patch-scale ablations and lung, soft-tissue, and bone evaluations. On 220 test slices from 31 patients, LBW-NPS reduces a local spectral gap related to the loss, on 64×64-pixel evaluation windows, by 31.9% relative to pooled band-weighted NPS, without a statistically significant PSNR change. This improvement is supported by lower errors relative to the reference in average NPS frequency and gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) measures not used in the loss, evaluated in homogeneous soft tissue. Local band-power matching therefore improves regional texture agreement without changing the denoising architecture.
entries.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027. Code: https://github.com/itu-biai/lbw-nps

entries.title: Life-IQA+: Boosting Blind Image Quality Assessment via GCN-enhanced Layer Interaction and Flexible Hierarchical Expert Specialization
entries.abstract: Blind image quality assessment (BIQA) is essential for evaluating and optimizing visual experience. Existing BIQA methods typically aggregate features from multiple backbone stages without accounting for their unequal contributions to quality prediction. Furthermore, uniformly supervising all experts may constrain their flexibility and limit the diversity of the learned quality representations. To address these issues, we present Life-IQA+, a quality representation decoding framework that combines graph convolutional network (GCN) enhanced layer interaction and flexible hierarchical expert specialization. Specifically, the layer interaction module constructs quality queries from GCN-refined deepest-stage features and uses penultimate-stage features as keys and values, thereby enabling cross-layer representation interaction via the cross-attention mechanism. Building on these representations, we further introduce a flexible hierarchical mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture comprising a densely activated shared expert layer and a sparsely activated routed expert layer. To enhance the representation diversity and ability of experts, we apply auxiliary classification supervision to a subset of shared experts using distortion-type labels for synthetic datasets and discretized quality-level labels for authentic datasets. Experiments on synthetic and authentic distortion benchmarks, together with controlled ablations of expert configurations and supervision strategies, show that Life-IQA+ achieves competitive prediction accuracy with a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost. The code is available at: https://github.com/TANGLONG2/Life-IQA-PlusPlus.

entries.title: Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Deep Learning for Prediction of Radiation-Induced Xerostomia in Head and Neck Cancer
entries.abstract: To develop and evaluate an uncertainty-aware multimodal learning framework for predicting radiation-induced xerostomia in patients receiving head-and-neck cancer radiotherapy. We developed a Bidirectional Attention-enhanced Diffusion Transformer (BA-DiT) that combines self-supervised multimodal representation learning with supervised Bayesian fine-tuning. The model integrates pretreatment CT images and three-dimensional dose distributions, focusing on bilateral parotid glands while incorporating surrounding anatomical and dosimetric information. During pretraining, bidirectional cross-attention integrates anatomical and dosimetric features, while a latent Diffusion Transformer learns joint representations through diffusion-based learning, feature reconstruction, and contrastive alignment. Supervised fine-tuning employs a Bayesian classifier to predict individualized xerostomia risk and quantify predictive uncertainty, with a learnable label-transition model accounting for potential toxicity label uncertainty. BA-DiT was developed using four independent cohorts (Moffitt, Emory, MSHS, and TCIA) and evaluated against baseline and ablation models. Evaluation included predictive performance, calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision curve analysis, and patient-level case studies. In independent MSHS and Emory cohorts, BA-DiT achieved AUCs of 0.83 and 0.80, respectively, outperforming baseline models. Predictive uncertainty peaked near the decision boundary, with aleatoric uncertainty being the predominant component. Uncertainty-based selective prediction generally improved net benefit among retained patients, with greater gains at lower prediction coverage. BA-DiT enables individualized xerostomia risk prediction while providing complementary uncertainty estimates, potentially supporting informed clinical decision-making and personalized toxicity management.

entries.title: AIstatLab at BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3: Quality-Controlled Consensus Pseudo-Labeling and Dense Expert Adaptation
entries.abstract: BraTS-GoAT Task 3 evaluates brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities using shared ET, TC, and WT regions. We present a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet trained with quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labels, a training-only nested-region objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers gener ated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases; fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening retained 983 for training with 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold ResEnc-M entry achieved mean DSC 0.834, mean NSD 0.510, and Acalc = 0.6720 on the validation server. Component effects were modest and region-dependent, with the clearest gains on ET. Source code is available at https://github.com/HeeSeung-Shin/Brats2026-Goat-HS.

entries.title: Breaking Noise Shortcuts in Self-Supervised Learning Via Noise-Aligned View Generation
entries.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is increasingly applied to scientific imaging domains, such as microscopy, where labels are scarce but noisy data is abundant. These domains exhibit significant signal-dependent noise, which can create a representational shortcut: since both augmented views derive from the same noisy image, the encoder can boost view agreement by also encoding noise patterns rather than semantic content. To enable noise-robust representation learning without knowledge of underlying noise models, we introduce Self-Aligned Noise Augmentation (SEANA), a drop-in module that generates noise-aware SSL views. SEANA learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform (VST) from noisy data, then estimates the clean signal and resamples independent noise in learned VST space, requiring no clean targets, no dataset-specific denoiser training or use at inference, and no changes to the SSL objective or encoder. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 under synthetic Gaussian, Poisson-Gaussian, and multiplicative noise, SEANA improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy across contrastive/non-contrastive SSL methods, indicating higher-quality representations. On real fluorescence imaging, SEANA improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by up to 28.6pp over standard SSL and 27.5pp over denoiser-preprocessed baselines. In all settings, SEANA outperforms the denoiser-preprocessed SSL pipelines, demonstrating that learned VST-space noise-aligned resampling yields more robust representations than denoising alone. Code is available at: https://github.com/opatil31/SEANA
entries.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

entries.title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
entries.abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g. MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

entries.title: Transferable Named Sparse Features for Morphology-based Gleason Grading
entries.abstract: Deep learning systems grade prostate biopsies at the level of pathologists, but most report a grade without the glandular architecture that justifies it. This work presents a grading system built on a sparse code over the tokens of a pathology foundation model. A sparse autoencoder pretrained on biopsies is aligned with multi-reader annotations, so that 69 of its 2048 features are named after Gleason morphologies such as cribriform glands, cords, and comedonecrosis. The same code feeds a grading network, which reads all features to predict Gleason patterns and the Grade Group, while morphology maps read directly from the named features. We evaluate the system on five public datasets that include needle biopsies, tissue-microarray cores, multi-reader annotations, and three scanners. The morphology maps remain stable across alignment runs and, without retraining, detect cribriform glands in external biopsies (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUROC, 0.849) and pattern 5 in unseen cores when evaluated by up to six pathologists (AUROC 0.846 to 0.919). In an independent biopsy cohort, Grade Group agreement with three pathologists on Leica scans is close to their agreement with each other. Removing the named features reduces the corresponding Gleason pattern predictions by 49% to 98%, with effects larger than those from 20 activity-matched random feature removals. These results show that a shared sparse representation can support competitive Gleason grading while providing named morphological evidence that transfers across datasets and whose contribution to grading can be measured directly.

entries.title: Joint Image Denoising and Interpolation via Mixed Graph Filtering
entries.abstract: Images often require both denoising and interpolation, yet treating the two tasks separately is suboptimal: interpolation introduces correlated noise that complicates subsequent denoising, while denoising may remove image details useful for interpolation. In this paper, we study joint image denoising and interpolation from a mixed graph filtering perspective, where denoising is modeled using undirected graph filters and interpolation using directed graph filters. We first establish that, under mild conditions, any (pseudo-)linear denoiser and interpolator can be interpreted as solution filters of maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation problems regularized by undirected and directed graph smoothness priors, respectively. Guided by these results, we formulate graph-based joint denoising and interpolation problems using both directed and undirected graph structures. We characterize when joint denoising/interpolation reduces to a separable pipeline and when a genuinely coupled optimization is required. For the non-separable case, we recover sparse graph operators from given denoisers and interpolators, yielding an efficient linear-system formulation solvable via conjugate gradient. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed joint framework consistently outperforms separate denoising and interpolation pipelines across multiple denoiser-interpolator combinations.

entries.title: Stochastic Optimisation for Scalable Ptychographic Image Reconstruction
entries.abstract: X-ray ptychography is a lensless coherent diffraction imaging technique capable of high spatial resolution, in which an image is reconstructed by solving a large-scale inverse problem from highly redundant far-field diffraction measurements acquired under overlapping illumination. Whilst the measurement redundancy created by overlapping illumination is essential for reconstruction fidelity, it leads to computational and memory demands that scale poorly with object size and target resolution when using conventional reconstruction algorithms. This work proposes a ptychographic reconstruction framework that reduces peak memory usage and time to convergence by leveraging stochastic optimisation techniques developed for large-scale machine learning. Specifically, the framework employs stochastic gradient descent with a decaying step size that progressively reduces the effect of gradient noise, referred to here as variance reduction (VR), with gradients that agree with automatic differentiation, to optimise the ptychographic forward model using randomly sampled subsets of diffraction measurements. For an experimental dataset of 200,000 diffraction patterns of 128×128 pixels, VR is demonstrated to require 65% of the peak GPU memory and 22% of the reconstruction time of the established maximum-likelihood (ML) algorithm. The VR framework incorporates the Poisson maximum-likelihood formulation and partial coherence within a unified and extensible optimisation setting. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the framework achieves reconstruction quality visually comparable to established methods, with lower peak GPU memory and a shorter time

entries.title: Micrograph B-factor estimation via Wilson statistics
entries.abstract: The single-particle cryo-electron microscopy imaging process is known to cause exponential decay in the amplitude and power spectra of proteins. This decay is modeled by the B factor and is currently corrected as a post-processing stage of the 3D reconstruction. As a consequence, all experimental images in the dataset are assumed to share the same B factor. In this paper, we suggest a novel approach wherein the B factor is determined and corrected as a preprocessing step to the reconstruction. We show such an approach can improve reconstruction resolution.

entries.title: Gaussian Splatoms: Direct Atomic Structure Identification in Electron Tomography
entries.abstract: Atomic electron tomography (AET) computationally reconstructs the 3D atomic structure of materials from a series of 2D projection measurements acquired at different tilt angles. Inspired by Gaussian splatting techniques from computer vision, we introduce an atom-centric parameterization for modeling AET samples. Instead of a conventional volumetric representation with a grid of voxels, we model the sample as a list of atoms, where each atom is a 3D Gaussian characterized by learned location, scale, and amplitude. The Gaussian model is a natural fit for atoms that allows us to easily incorporate prior information grounded in physics; we impose isotropy of atoms, a minimum interatomic distance, and realistic atomic radii. We show in simulation that our method is more robust than volumetric baselines to real-world imaging challenges, including a limited number of measurements and low electron dose. We further show that our method yields a more physically plausible reconstruction of an experimental 23,000 atom iron-platinum nanoparticle than a previously published volumetric reconstruction. Beyond tomography, our representation is a promising tool for any atomic resolution imaging modality (e.g. multislice electron ptychography).

entries.title: LIC-Audit: How Comparable Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression?
entries.abstract: Learned image compression (LIC) papers often report BD-rate improvements of only a few percent. They are measured against VTM reference software whose version keeps changing: the claims we audit name 7 versions, 5 in 2025 papers alone. But how comparable are these numbers across papers, and what evidence should future papers give for such small gains? We introduce LIC-Audit, an analysis of 353 released rate-distortion curves from 36 repositories, and a controlled re-evaluation of eight public codec releases with 28,193 encode-decode records. We identify three problems. First, different VTM reference runs change BD-rates by up to 3.56 percentage points, and on CLIC Pro published numbers order 10 of 55 method pairs differently from a common computation; comparing codecs directly over a fixed quality range removes this dependence. Second, releases use different and mostly undocumented conventions for counting bits, computing PSNR, and padding images. Under consistent measurement, the GLIC method's 1.00% lead over the HPCM method on Tecnick becomes a 1.43% deficit, changing only the padding reverses the comparison of HPCM and CMIC, and most gaps narrow when MS-SSIM replaces PSNR. Third, average curves hide how much results vary from image to image, so whether a small gain is statistically significant depends on the assumed variation. An optimistic assumption calls 12.0% of comparisons between equally good codecs significant on test sets as small as Kodak, instead of 5%; a cautious one leaves 18 of 45 differences between recent codecs undecided, yet per-image results show 12 of them to be significant. Beyond auditing past results, LIC-Audit provides a versioned evaluation protocol, a public leaderboard website with a scoring tool, source-linked benchmark data, per-image measurements, and reporting guidelines, to help future LIC papers make comparable and verifiable claims of progress.

entries.title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
entries.abstract: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.

entries.title: Streaming Generative Video Compression with Embedding Alignment and In-Context Propagation
entries.abstract: Video compression at ultra-low bitrates presents substantial challenges in preserving perceptual quality. Although pretrained video diffusion transformers (DiTs) provide powerful generative priors, existing generative video compression (GVC) methods built on them typically rely on computationally expensive VAE decoders to reconstruct video frames. Moreover, jointly refining multiple frames to exploit the inherent spatiotemporal modeling capabilities of video DiTs introduces additional buffering delay. To address these challenges, we propose SGVC, a streaming generative video compression framework that adapts a pretrained latent video DiT into a causal pixel-space refiner. Specifically, SGVC projects decoded features from a contextual pixel codec directly into the DiT input embedding space. To bridge the representation gap between codec-derived embeddings and pretrained DiT embeddings, we introduce Embedding Alignment, which aligns the projected embeddings with input embeddings extracted from the original frames during training. The refined DiT hidden states are then mapped directly to the pixel domain through a lightweight reconstruction path, bypassing the pretrained VAE decoder. To further exploit the spatiotemporal priors of the video DiT while maintaining causal decoding, we introduce In-Context Propagation, which reuses layer-wise K/V states across frames to exploit historical generative context, improving temporal consistency without requiring clip-wise buffering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVC achieves competitive rate-perception performance, with average BD-rate savings of 71.97% over S²VC in terms of DISTS. Project Page: https://chigland.github.io/SGVC/
entries.comment: 15 pages, 18 figures, 5 tables, including supplementary material

entries.title: SWIMSS: An Open Multi-Center SwinUNETR Model for Multiple Sclerosis White Matter Lesion Segmentation
entries.abstract: Purpose: To develop and validate SWIMSS (SWInUNETR for Multiple Sclerosis white matter lesion Segmentation), a SwinUNETR-based deep learning (DL) model for reliable automated white matter (WM) lesion segmentation, in a large multicentric cohort of people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS). Methods: A real-world longitudinal dataset of 1,385 pwMS from seven Swiss clinical centers was used to train, validate, and test SWIMSS and two state-of-the-art DL architectures: UNETR and MSSegDiff. Inference results obtained with LST-AI were also compared. Preprocessed magnetization-prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI sequences, acquired with various MR systems and field strengths, served as model inputs. Model performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: SWIMSS achieved the highest performance, with a DSC of 81.37 (95% CI: 80.63-82.11), outperforming UNETR (79.06; 95% CI: 78.33-79.79), MSSegDiff (75.70; 95% CI: 74.97-76.43), and LST-AI (63.19; 95% CI: 62.08-64.30). Normalized DSC followed a similar trend, with SWIMSS reaching 84.88. Lesion detection F1 achieved 81.14. Statistical analyses confirmed its superior performance (p < 0.001). Conclusion: SWIMSS achieved state-of-the-art performance for WM lesion segmentation. By making this model publicly available, we enable broader access to high-quality segmentation tools, allowing smaller centers, often lacking large annotated datasets or computational resources, to benefit from a model trained on a diverse, large-scale cohort. This promotes more equitable access to advanced imaging analysis and supports reproducibility and standardization in MS research.

entries.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval
entries.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.

entries.title: Beyond Accuracy: Benchmarking Uncertainty Quantification in Retinal Disease Screening
entries.abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for evaluating retinal AI systems beyond classification accuracy, yet it remains unclear whether existing UQ strategies generalize across diseases, model architectures, and reliability criteria. We introduce a large-scale, multi-disease benchmark comprising over 242,000 fundus photographs from 32 datasets covering diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and glaucoma. We evaluate six representative UQ strategies across three Vision Transformer configurations, assessing discrimination, probabilistic calibration, selective prediction, and conformal prediction-set coverage. Our findings reveal no universally superior model or UQ strategy: methods that improve reliability in one disease or architecture may underperform in another, while improvements in discrimination, calibration, and selective prediction do not necessarily align. Notably, computationally intensive methods do not consistently outperform simple confidence scores, and domain-specific foundation models and calibration-oriented loss functions do not guarantee greater reliability. In contrast, conformal prediction provides a complementary framework for achieving near-nominal marginal prediction-set coverage across diverse settings, subject to its statistical assumptions. These findings challenge universal UQ recommendations and highlight the need for disease-specific, model-specific, and multidimensional reliability evaluation before clinical deployment. We release standardized dataset splits, trained checkpoints, evaluation code, and an interactive research demonstration to support reproducible benchmarking.

entries.title: MedImgAnnotator: batch wise medical image annotation and preprocessing tool
entries.abstract: The curation of large cohort datasets for developing deep learning models demands annotating or editing over the AI-predicted labels. However, openly available annotation tools are time-consuming, as they involve complex navigational steps and do not support batch processing. This study aimed to develop a simple, fast, semiautomated batch-annotation tool named MedImgAnnotator. The tool was created by integrating editing tools, image mask pair matching logic, preprocessing functions, object detection tool, and a plugin management system. Its performance was evaluated in terms of active annotation time and ease of use by the developer and 12 users using open-source MR and CT scans. Additionally, the tool had been used by the MICCAI 2026 CARE Challenge liver segmentation best performance winner to annotate liver masks from 6412 MRI volumes. The evaluation results showed that MedImgAnnotator reduced active annotation time from 206.5+/-32.87 (average active annotation time of openly available tools) seconds to 59 seconds. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test of 12 users evaluation results recorded P values of 0.032 and 0.008 for the active annotation time and higher ease of use rating metrics, respectively, indicating that the current tool significantly reduces annotation time and enhances ease of use. Moreover, the tool utilization for annotating different regions of interest from different modality scans and body regions shows its usability across modalities and areas of interest. MedImgAnnotator, which significantly reduces active annotation time for large imaging cohorts, is available as an executable file and as a Python script. Access link: https://ewunateassaye.github.io/developed-tools/medimgannotator.html

entries.title: Virtual EMI Receiver Generation (VERGE) for Improved EMI Removal in MRI
entries.abstract: MRI is not designed to operate in the presence of EMI emitting electronic devices. To accomodate this, we propose VERGE which improves on previous EMI removal methods and can operate without external EMI sensors. VERGE estimates a reference coil non-linearly from all imaging and non-imaging coils by training a small per-scan convolutional neural net to generate a virtual coil. The virtual coil is then used with STRIDE, a reference-based EMI removal method. For single-source EMI contamination, VERGE performed similarly to the reference method. For multi-source dynamic EMI contamination, VERGE outperformed the comparison methods. Notably, VERGE with zero physical EMI sensors outperformed the comparison methods even with two physical EMI sensors. A non-linearly estimated virtual EMI coil improves reference-coil-based EMI removal under dynamic multi-source EMI, and enables effective EMI removal without physical EMI sensors or training data.

entries.title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
entries.abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning T₁w, FLAIR and T₂w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.
entries.comment: 25 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables (8-page main text with appendices). Code: https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer

entries.title: SCAN: Site-Aware Collaborative Privacy-Preserving Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Neurological Disease Classification
entries.abstract: Worldwide neuroimaging data could strengthen diagnostic foundation models, but privacy rules often prevent centralizing brain MRI scans. We present SCAN, a site-aware collaborative adaptation framework for Neurological Disease Classification that lets new sites adapt a 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) without retraining or sharing patient scans. Each site keeps exact class prototypes for local prediction and can share privacy-protected class summaries: norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise. Using 7,641 scans from 67 sites across 12 countries, covering Alzheimer's disease (AD), stroke, epilepsy and controls, we assess local adaptation, cross-site benefits, and effects on existing sites. At seven unseen sites, the frozen VLM's zero-shot AUCs were 0.833-0.945 for AD and stroke. Training-free local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863, nearly matching a classifier trained at each site (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759). With differential privacy (ε = 4), new sites contributed without materially reducing accuracy at existing sites (AUC change ≤0.2%), although gains from sharing were limited, and membership attacks performed near chance. SCAN offers hospitals a worldwide framework to adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging scans or retraining.

entries.title: How Much Does Saliency Accuracy Matter for Saliency-Guided 360-degree Image Compression?
entries.abstract: Saliency-guided coding allocates bits to the regions viewers are most likely to attend, but accurate 360-degree saliency prediction is computationally expensive, an obstacle for low-latency immersive streaming applications such as robot teleoperation. We quantify how much saliency-prediction accuracy actually translates into compression gain. Building on a saliency-guided rate-distortion-optimized (RDO) learned codec, modified so that the training-time latent mask is driven by ground-truth saliency, which yields a single, predictor-agnostic codec, we evaluate saliency predictors spanning two orders of magnitude in compute on both the learned codec and H.265/HEVC. The results show that higher saliency-prediction accuracy yields diminishing compression gains: a lightweight predictor fast enough for live use (52 frames per second) captures 65% of the ground-truth oracle's bit-rate saving, a 3.3x heavier one reaches 74%, and a further 38x increase in compute adds no measurable benefit, on either codec. Therefore, lightweight predictors might also be a practical choice for latency-constrained 360-degree streaming.
entries.comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)

entries.title: Investigating the Benefit of Transfer Learning from the Locus Coeruleus for Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta Segmentation
entries.abstract: The substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) is a small midbrain nucleus that degenerates early in Parkinson's disease (PD). T1-weighted FLASH MRI enables its visualization and may support early detection of neurodegeneration. However, manual segmentation is difficult and time-consuming, and deep learning models often suffer from the limited availability of labeled data. Transfer learning (TL) may help by adapting pre-trained models to small datasets. We investigate whether TL from a model trained on the locus coeruleus (LC), a nucleus with a similar appearance in this sequence, improves SNpc segmentation. Several TL strategies were evaluated using a 3D U-Net. With as few as 5-14 labeled subjects, TL and training from scratch achieved similar performance, reaching a Dice similarity coefficient of up to 0.77, close to reported inter-rater agreement. No TL strategy differed significantly from training from scratch, suggesting that initialization from the LC offers no significant benefit for SNpc segmentation.
entries.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027

entries.title: Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
entries.abstract: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.

entries.title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
entries.abstract: The blind perspective-n-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation–maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by 5–170× relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.
entries.comment: 65 pages, including references and appendices; under review

entries.title: Dynamic infrared thermography and computed tomography angiography fusion for DIEP flap perforator selection: a novel measurement system
entries.abstract: Accurate perforator selection is critical for successful deep inferior epigastric artery perforator (DIEP) flap breast reconstruction. While computed tomography angiography (CTA) provides high-resolution anatomical detail, it lacks functional perfusion assessment. Dynamic infrared thermography (DIRT), in contrast, captures superficial rewarming dynamics but lacks objective anatomical validation. This study presents a standardized multimodal measurement system enabling automated fusion of DIRT with CTA-derived perforator coordinates. The framework integrates controlled thermographic acquisition, real-time hotspot detection, metric spatial calibration, and global one-to-one assignment of thermal hotspots to CTA perforators within a predefined periumbilical region of interest. The workflow was evaluated in 12 patients. Of 46 CTA perforators within the region of interest, 84.8% were successfully linked to thermographic hotspots, with a median spatial offset of 14.74 mm. Automated assignment excluded 76.1% of detected hotspots due to lack of anatomical correspondence, thereby reducing subjective interpretation. The proposed system enables quantitative multimodal validation of functional and anatomical imaging and provides objective support for perforator selection in clinical practice.
entries.journalRef: 2026 IEEE Medical Measurements & Applications (MeMeA), Montevideo, Uruguay, 2026, pp. 1-6

entries.title: VoxSAOR: Semantic-Aware Occupancy Robustification via Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling
entries.abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction provides a dense semantic representation of scenes for autonomous driving and embodied perception, yet remains vulnerable to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that induce spatially varying reliability in voxel features. Existing methods typically map voxel representations to semantic predictions without explicitly modeling such observation-induced feature variations. To address this limitation, we propose VoxSAOR, a semantic-aware occupancy robustification framework that models aleatoric uncertainty through feature-space proxies. It first quantifies Local Semantic Consistency (LSC) to derive a voxel-wise structural stability prior and uses cross-view semantic consensus to filter unreliable semantic correspondences. Within each semantic category, spatially matched stable and ambiguous voxels form stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions, which are modeled by a class-conditional diagonal Gaussian distribution, capturing both feature displacement and dispersion. Guided by these proxy distributions, Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning (AREL) trains independently parameterized prediction heads using feature perturbations at progressively increasing scales, with perturbation strength modulated by structural reliability. At inference, proxy modeling and sampling are disabled, and all heads process the same observed features; their output probabilities are then averaged to produce a deterministic consensus prediction without requiring sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of VoxSAOR in improving semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/VoxSAOR.
entries.comment: The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/VoxSAOR

entries.title: Signs of Wear: Evaluating Intelligent Speed Assistance Under Synthetic Adverse Conditions
entries.abstract: Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA) systems rely on cameras to recognize speed-limit signs, yet existing benchmarks underrepresent the weathered, dirty, and overgrown signs commonly encountered on rural roads. We use generative image editing to introduce different forms of wear into real street-level images of speed-limit signs. The resulting ISA-Wear dataset contains paired original and edited images. Guided by text instructions, a multimodal image-editing model adds snow, rust, vegetation, faded paint, or mud to the speed-limit sign in a street-level frame at three severity levels. Where appropriate, the surrounding scene is adapted as well, and the viewpoint is kept. Every edited frame has an unedited counterpart, and we only evaluate frames whose original is recognized correctly, so any failure can be attributed to the wear. Since the model alters the sign's geometry in 21% of the edits, all edits are filtered by a geometric check and a manual review. Severity is measured as the LPIPS distance between the original and the edited sign plate. On 716 worn frames, we find that in detect-then-read pipelines, wear breaks detection before it breaks reading. The detector finds only 62% of the worn signs, even though it finds every one of them in the original frames. Missed detections account for 78–87% of failed reads, a pattern that a zero-shot detector shares. Given the annotated sign box, as in the crop-based benchmarks, a classifier still reads 78% of the worn signs, but only 56% when it has to rely on the detector

entries.title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
entries.abstract: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).
entries.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ISBI 2027

entries.title: Streaming across viewing conditions - The effect of viewing distance and display luminance on video quality
entries.abstract: The visibility of streamed video distortions is affected by the user's display and viewing conditions, such as their display's luminance or the viewing distance. Distortions become less visible at lower luminance levels or farther viewing distances. However, most image and video quality metrics assume fixed optimal display and viewing conditions, making them insensitive to the viewing conditions. In this work, we demonstrate how existing metrics can be adapted to account for both factors and compare such an adaptation with the metrics that natively model viewing conditions. First, we collected a new video quality dataset, HDR-VDC, which contains streaming distortions in 4K HDR videos. The dataset consists of 12 4K and 4 FHD HDR source video content, each distorted with AV1 encoding and Lanczos upscaling from a lower resolution. The quality loss due to the distortions was measured at two viewing distances, corresponding to 60 and 120 pixels per visual degree, and two display mean luminance levels, varying by a factor of 8 in terms of luminance. Next, we developed a pre-processing framework that lets us adapt many quality metrics so that they can evaluate content across the viewing distances and luminance levels. The framework employs a display model and perceptually uniform encoding, PU21, to account for the effect of display luminance, and perspective projection scaling (PPS) to account for the effect of viewing distance. We used the framework to compare the performance of 35 state-of-the-art metrics. This allowed us to identify a selection of existing quality metrics that can be effectively adapted to account for the viewing conditions.

entries.title: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks
entries.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated digital content generation and intensified concerns around fraud, misuse, counterfeiting, and content provenance. Defensive image watermarking provides a practical mechanism for identifying and tracing digital content, but recent watermark-removal attacks challenge its robustness. This study investigates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), which combines HiDDeN and StegaStamp as complementary non-semantic and semantic watermarking schemes. Using 50 images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ, both embedding orders are evaluated, followed by UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially. Results show that both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding, with only limited embedding-order effects. Under individual attacks, one watermark generally remains strongly decodable: StegaStamp under the non-semantic attack and HiDDeN under the semantic attack. Sequential attacks are therefore required to substantially reduce both watermark signals, while attack order has a limited and configuration-dependent effect. The semantic attack also shows a broader effect across the two watermark types than the non-semantic attack. LPIPS remains relatively low in several settings, although qualitative inspection reveals noticeable distortions, particularly in selected facial images, indicating that LPIPS should not be used alone to assess visual quality. Overall, the findings show that combining complementary watermark types can increase robustness against single-stage removal attacks and motivate broader multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual evaluation, and further study of sequential watermark-removal strategies.
entries.comment: 13 pages, 16 figures. Preprint based on M.Sc. thesis research

entries.title: Machine Learning for Near Real-Time Identification of Wildfire Burned Areas
entries.abstract: In this article, we present a near real-time method that estimates burned probability anywhere in the world using satellite images. Our approach takes advantage of the state-of-the-art pix2pix model to translate a preprocessed index calculated from Landsat 8/9 images into an approximate of USGS Burn Probability indicating per pixel burn probability. Since this is a machine learning-based approach, it can be automated with a minimum amount of human intervention with significantly less time delays and geographic restrictions compared to other contemporary methods. We include results from our experiments and compare our approximation with the USGS Burn Probability using RMSE score.

entries.title: Equal Dose, Different Coverage:Tracing Rate and Duration in Image Editing
entries.abstract: Benchmarks for scientific image editing test whether a model draws the outcome of a described process, leaving open which representations carry its errors and whether correcting them yields the right quantity. We study this question with an airbrush of fixed deposition profile, under which exchanging rate and duration preserves the dose and should preserve the endpoint, yet changes the edited coverage. Matched-norm activation patches across text positions and denoising stages show that, in distilled FLUX with Chinese prompts, representations at unchanged text positions (context) carry this discrepancy: early context transfers 3.51 of the 3.98 percentage-point (pp) signed route difference, against 0.09 pp for equal-norm updates at the two changed digits. Early image latents transmit native (unpatched) route differences across two FLUX configurations and OmniGen, while text-position effects depend on configuration. The trace predicts an intervention: share early context between routes while each retains its own digits. On independent English layouts, this reduces the distilled-FLUX absolute route gap from 1.13 to 0.60 pp, outperforms early digit sharing, and improves agreement more than in base FLUX under directly paired tests. Calibrated evaluation, which prescribes an area for each dose, separates this gain from accuracy: sharing the full prompt encoding produces identical route images with target errors of 8-16 pp, and stating the target percentage directly retains a compressed area response. Localization predicts a consistency gain on new layouts, and calibration measures the quantity error that agreement leaves unresolved.

entries.title: XLSAR-Bench: Towards Extremely Large SAR Imagery Understanding of MLLMs
entries.abstract: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has highlighted the need for comprehensive benchmarks to assess their capabilities and limitations in remote sensing (RS). However, evaluating MLLMs in large-size synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scenarios remains challenging, as understanding complete scenes requires both global semantic interpretation and fine-grained target perception. Existing SAR benchmarks predominantly rely on small image patches, limiting their ability to assess these capabilities jointly. To address these limitations, we present XLSAR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the perception and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in large-scene SAR imagery. XLSAR-Bench comprises 405 images with an average size of 7153×7153 pixels, ten tasks spanning visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning, with all evaluation samples meticulously annotated manually, assisted by a semi-automatic captioner. Experimental results from general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs reveal persistent challenges in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately perceiving small targets. We have open-sourced XLSAR-Bench to support further research in developing more powerful MLLMs for complete large SAR scenes.

entries.title: Ref-MIL: Plug-and-Play Posterior Refinement for Multiple Instance Learning in QSM-Based Brain Disease Classification
entries.abstract: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) is a novel quantitative MRI contrast for studying tissue susceptibility changes in brain disorders, including Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple sclerosis (MS). However, small cohorts and the lack of local annotations make developing deep learning models for QSM-based diagnosis challenging. In this work, we propose PoRef-MIL, a weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) framework combining iterative slice relabeling and network retraining with a plug-and-play posterior refinement module (PRM). During training, a 2D dual-branch diagnosis network and a subject-level classifier were alternately trained for five rounds. The classifier was used to update slice pseudo-labels for retraining the diagnosis network. The PRM was applied during inference to refine slice probabilities through bidirectional posterior inference and calculate entropy-derived confidence from the refined probabilities, which was then used in sliding-window scoring to obtain subject-level predictions. PoRef-MIL was evaluated on an in-house PD cohort of 287 participants and a public MS cohort of 150 participants. Compared with eight classification methods, PoRef-MIL achieved the highest mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.942 and 0.872, and accuracies of 0.926 and 0.833, for PD and MS classification, respectively. Ablation experiments were conducted to validate the effectiveness of iterative relabeling and PRM, and the plug-and-play feature of the proposed PRM was also evaluated using four state-of-the-art MIL models. Overall, PoRef-MIL offers a promising approach to QSM-based disease classification in small cohorts without manual slice annotations.

entries.title: Zero-shot diffusion image compression with sectioned codebooks and one channel code
entries.abstract: Zero-shot diffusion codecs such as Turbo-DDCM compress images without any training. In each coded step, the encoder selects noise vectors from one codebook and transmits a single index for the selected set. We propose sectioned codebooks. A coded step is divided into sections, and each section has its own large codebook and transmits its best vector as a short field of bits. A model based on order statistics quantifies how well the bits of a step are used and predicts the gain of sectioned codebooks from measurements of Turbo-DDCM alone. Fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms make sections of 2²⁰ vectors practical. At equal bits, sectioned codebooks improve the PSNR of Turbo-DDCM by 0.18 to 0.51 dB on three datasets, improve LPIPS and DISTS, and save 16 to 21% of the bits at equal PSNR. Codecs that are robust to channel errors by design are usually compared only with unprotected codecs. We compare them, at equal total bits, with a codec protected by one channel code. With one BCH code, the sectioned codec outperforms all reported results of Robust Turbo-DDCM and BitFlat on two datasets, by up to 7.74 dB at the highest bit error rate. At the lowest bit error rate its margin over BitFlat is only 0.08 to 0.16 dB. When the code fails, the receiver can still decode the fields as received. Additional experiments cover burst errors and packet loss, and all observed gains of robust codecs stay within a limit derived from the channel capacity.

entries.title: Midsagittal Corpus Callosum Parameterization: A Framework for Spatially Detailed Diffusion MR Imaging Analysis
entries.abstract: The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest white matter structure in the human brain and plays a central role in interhemispheric communication. Diffusion MR imaging is widely used to investigate microstructural organization, but commonly used analysis approaches have important limitations. Voxel-based methods rely heavily on accurate inter-subject registration and smoothing choices, tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) restricts the analysis to a narrow white matter skeleton, and parcellation approaches reduce spatial detail by averaging diffusion measures over relatively large regions. In this work, we introduce a parameterization framework for the analysis of the midsagittal CC that resamples the structure using a standardized grid of points, establishing a geometric correspondence across individuals without explicit inter-subject registration. In a test-retest dataset, the method provided stable measurements while covering most of the midsagittal CC, and sensitivity analyses showed that results in the central CC changed little under perturbations of the input CC mask, whereas peripheral regions were more sensitive. The framework was further evaluated in group analyses of aging and Alzheimer's disease in datasets that differ in acquisition protocol and spatial resolution. Effect-size maps and quantitative comparisons showed that its results were largely consistent with TBSS and parcellation-based analyses in the overall spatial pattern of effects, while also revealing additional spatially localized differences. These findings suggest that the parameterization provides a simple, computationally efficient, and spatially detailed approach for investigating midsagittal CC microstructure, offering a structure-specific complement to whole-brain and region-based methods.
entries.comment: 47 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables, plus 11 pages of supplementary material (12 figures, 6 tables). Under review at Imaging Neuroscience

entries.title: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models
entries.abstract: Violation-of-expectation (VOE) benchmarks evaluate intuitive physics in video world models by testing whether physically impossible events produce greater prediction errors than matched possible events. However, conventional VOE evaluations aggregate prediction errors across space and time, making it unclear whether successful discrimination reflects model's understanding of physical violations at the locations and time where they occur. To address this limitation, we introduce localized VOE evaluation, a framework that measures prediction error differences between possible and impossible events within spatial regions and temporal intervals associated with physical violations. We compare global, temporally localized, and spatiotemporally localized evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric videos or large-scale natural video datasets. Our results reveal that global and localized judgments can diverge in both directions: global aggregation can either obscure correct localized discrimination or produce apparent discrimination without corresponding localized evidence. During continued pretraining on developmental egocentric videos, agreement between global and localized judgments changes non-monotonically, while confidence in localized judgments increases despite modest improvements in accuracy. Together, these findings establish localized VOE evaluation as a complementary diagnostic for assessing intuitive physics in video world models and demonstrate that global prediction errors do not necessarily reflect the spatiotemporal evidence of physical violations.

entries.title: Learned Regularization for Sparse-View CT: Accuracy, Lesion Detectability and Distribution Shift of a Plug-and-Play Prior against Tuned Total Variation
entries.abstract: Learned image priors are often proposed to replace hand-crafted regularizers in sparse-view computed tomography (CT), yet they are usually judged by PSNR on data resembling their training set. We evaluate one noise-conditioned DnCNN denoiser used as a Plug-and-Play prior against filtered back-projection (FBP), Tikhonov and total-variation (TV) regularization, with every method tuned on validation data and all differences paired. On synthetic 28x28 digit images, the prior beats box-constrained TV by about 3.4 dB at moderate noise (sigma = 0.05, 20 angles), but the advantage shrinks at low noise and reverses under distribution shift: an MNIST-trained prior is 3.1 dB (Fashion-MNIST) and 4.3-4.6 dB (Shepp-Logan phantom) below TV, whereas a Fashion-MNIST-trained prior beats TV by 2.2 dB on Fashion-MNIST, consistent with prior mismatch rather than a failure of PnP itself. In a lesion-insertion test the prior detects lesions worse than TV in distribution despite its higher PSNR, and under mismatch it produces more lesion-like false blobs than box-constrained TV for seven of eight lesion types. On real LoDoPaB-CT slices (patient-disjoint split; 30, 60 and 120 angles; three dose levels; 40 test patients), the prior does not consistently outperform a well-tuned TV in PSNR (-0.93 to +0.33 dB) and has lower SSIM in eight of nine conditions. Its lesion-detection AUC is higher than this TV's in all nine conditions (significant in six) but never significantly higher than that of Hann-filtered FBP, which the PSNR-tuned TV falls below in detection in all nine conditions (seven significant). On non-anatomical phantoms its PSNR falls below TV in all six conditions. PSNR and lesion detectability thus rank the methods differently. Our conclusions concern one small denoiser, and the CT analysis was developed after seeing results, without pre-specified primary comparisons.
